parole.significato: A musical note one beat long in 4/4 time.
parole.testo: From Middle English crochet, from Old French crochet (“small hook”), from croc + -et (diminutive suffix), from Old Norse krókr (“hook”). The musical note was named so because of a small hook on its stem in black notation (in modern notation this hook is on the quaver/eighth note). Doublet of crochet

parole.significato: The top of the rump of a horse or other quadruped.
parole.testo: From Middle English croupe, from Old French croupe (“rump, body”), from Old Norse kroppr (“body, trunk, mass”), from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz (“body, mass, heap, collection, crop”), from Proto-Indo-European *grewb- (“to curve, bend, crawl”). More at crupper, doublet of croupe, group, and crop.

parole.significato: The triangular area at the peak of an external wall adjacent to, and terminating, two sloped roof surfaces (pitches).
parole.testo: The southern English term gable probably came from Old French gable (compare modern French gâble), from Old Norse gafl. The northern form gavel is perhaps also akin to Old Norse gafl, masculine, of the same meaning (compare Swedish gavel, Danish gavl). See gafl for more etymology information.

parole.significato: An establishment that breeds horses; a stud farm.
parole.testo: From Middle English haras, from Old French haraz, probably from Old Norse.

parole.significato: To inhabit or to visit frequently (most often used in reference to ghosts).
parole.testo: From Middle English haunten (“to reside, inhabit, use, employ”), from Old French hanter (“to inhabit, frequent, resort to”), from Old Northern French hanter (“to go back home, frequent”), from Old Norse heimta (“to bring home, fetch”) or/and from Old English hāmettan (“to bring home; house; cohabit

parole.significato: A piece of ivory, generally from a marine mammal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Middle English rewell bon, ruel bon (“walrus ivory”), from Old French roal, rohal (“walrus ivory”), ultimately from Old Norse hrosshvalr (“walrus”).

parole.significato: A small medieval bag used to carry food, money, utensils etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English scrippe, an aphetism of Old French escrepe (“purse, alms-bag”), a variant of escharpe, from Old Norse skreppa. Cognate with Danish skreppe (“scrip”), Norwegian skreppa (“bag”). Doublet of scarf.

parole.significato: To put something (such as a coin) into a slot (narrow aperture).
parole.testo: From Middle English slot, from Old French esclot, likely from Old Norse slóð (“track”). As a gambling machine, via clipping of slot machine. Compare sleuth.
